summary: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) was a missing bounds check in OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension. A malformed request could make a server return up to 64 KiB of memory, which could contain private keys, passwords and session cookies. A fixed version, 1.0.1g, was released on 7 April 2014.

overview.background: OpenSSL implements TLS for much of the web. Versions 1.0.1 through 1.0.1f had the flaw. Builds compiled with the heartbeat option disabled were not affected.
systems: Web servers and other services using that library
overview.impact: Servers could leak up to 64 KiB of memory per request, potentially including private keys and user data.
overview.severity: Critical. Wikipedia reports that by 9 May 2014 only 43 percent of affected sites had reissued certificates (Netcraft).
overview.gaps: This file uses Wikipedia as the readable source; heartbleed.com (the card source) could not be read.

timeline.e: The flawed code enters OpenSSL's repository.
Neel Mehta of Google reports the bug privately to OpenSSL.
The bug is publicly disclosed and OpenSSL 1.0.1g is released.
Operators patch, restart, and reissue certificates. By 9 May, 43 percent of affected sites had done so, per Netcraft.

rootCause.trigger: A missing bounds check in the TLS heartbeat extension.
rootCause.underlying: A malformed request could make the server return more memory than the payload it was sent.
contributing: The code was in a very widely used library
Memory contents are not controlled by the attacker, so any secret may leak
Many operators patched but did not reissue keys

evidence.label: Fixed version
evidence.body: A fixed version of OpenSSL was released on 7 April 2014

evidence.label: Slow certificate reissue
evidence.body: only 43% of affected web sites had reissued their security certificates

diagnose.step: Check which processes use the library.
Check whether heartbeat is compiled out.

correct.why: Old memory images are still vulnerable.

correct.step: Reissue keys and certificates and revoke the old ones.

prevent.step: Keep an inventory of crypto libraries.

fix.safety: Do not test other people's servers without permission.

troubleshoot.scenario: A critical OpenSSL bug is announced. You run hundreds of services and some use the library statically.
troubleshoot.question: How do you respond?
hints: How do you find all users of the library?
In what order do you patch?
troubleshoot.answer: Inventory, patch internet-facing services first, restart everything that loaded the library, then reissue keys and rotate secrets.

design.prompt: Design a fast response to a library vulnerability.
design.answer: SBOM, central patch pipeline, automated certificates, canary and rollout.

checks.q: How much memory per request could leak?
